passages.t: The Sabbath, Passover and Unleavened Bread
passages.happening:
“These are My appointed feasts, the feasts of the LORD that you are to proclaim as sacred assemblies” (verse 2).

First, every week: “For six days work may be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of complete rest, a day of sacred assembly” (verse 3).

Then the year. “The Passover to the LORD begins at twilight on the fourteenth day of the first month” (verse 5). The next day the Feast of Unleavened Bread begins. “For seven days you must eat unleavened bread” (verse 6). On its first and seventh days the people gather and do no regular work (verses 7-8).
passages.hearers:
Leviticus has made places holy, and people. Now it makes time holy. This chapter is Israel's calendar.

God calls the feasts ‘My appointed feasts’. The Hebrew word, mo'ed, comes from a root meaning to appoint or to meet. It is related to the name of the Tent of Meeting. The feasts are God's appointments with his people. They are times he sets to meet them. They are not holidays Israel made up for itself.

Each feast day is called a ‘sacred assembly’, a day when the people are called together. The phrase comes eleven times. Holiness here is kept in company.

The list begins with the Sabbath. Before any yearly feast there is the weekly one, and the yearly feasts are built on its pattern. The number seven runs through the whole chapter: the seventh day, seven days of unleavened bread, seven weeks, the seventh month, seven days of booths.

The months followed the moon. The first month falls in March or April, when the barley harvest begins.

Passover remembered the night God rescued Israel from Egypt. The week of bread made without leaven remembered the haste in which they left. Each feast joined a memory to a harvest.

On whether Christians should keep a Sabbath, and how, Christians differ. The note on Exodus 16:22-30 sets out the views, and these notes take no side.
passages.later:
The feast was given on the night of the rescue itself: “this day will be a memorial for you, and you are to celebrate it as a feast to the LORD, as a permanent statute for the generations to come” (Exodus 12:14).

Jesus said of the weekly day of rest, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27).

Jesus died at Passover, and Paul draws the line himself: “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). That line does not take Passover from the Jewish people, who keep it to this day as their own remembrance of what God did for them.
passages.asks: God set appointments in the week and the year to meet his people. Ask what fixed times you keep for God, alone and with others, and what tends to crowd them out. And ask whether you can stop work for a day and trust that the world will hold.

passages.t: The first sheaf, and the Feast of Weeks
passages.happening:
When Israel is in the land and reaps its harvest, “you are to bring to the priest a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest” (verse 10). The priest lifts it before the LORD. No one eats bread or new grain until this has been done (verse 14).

From that day they count seven full weeks. “You shall count off fifty days until the day after the seventh Sabbath, and then present an offering of new grain to the LORD” (verse 16). They bring two loaves ‘baked with leaven’, with burnt offerings, a sin offering and a peace offering (verses 17-19).

And in the middle of the harvest laws: “When you reap the harvest of your land, do not reap all the way to the edges of your field or gather the gleanings of your harvest. Leave them for the poor and the foreign resident” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
These two feasts mark the grain harvest, barley first and wheat seven weeks later.

The first sheaf cut was brought to God before anyone ate from the new crop. Giving the first part said that the whole harvest was his gift, and it trusted him for the rest.

Fifty days on came the Feast of Weeks. The two loaves were baked with leaven. This was ordinary bread, the bread of daily life, given back to God. Greek-speaking Jews later called the feast Pentecost, from the Greek word for fiftieth.

Then verse 22. A reader who has come through chapter 19 knows it. The law of leaving the edges of the field is repeated here, in the middle of the calendar. The harvest festival must not forget the people who have no harvest of their own. Israel was not to thank God for plenty with full hands and closed fields.

One detail was argued over in the time of Jesus. ‘The day after the Sabbath’ in verse 11 was read by the Pharisees as the day after the first day of the feast, and by the Sadducees as the Sunday after the weekly Sabbath. The two readings gave different dates for the Feast of Weeks.

Later Jewish tradition linked this feast, Shavuot, with the giving of the law at Sinai.
passages.later:
Ruth gleaned in the fields of Boaz from the barley harvest to the wheat harvest, the weeks this passage counts. Boaz told his men, “Even if she gathers among the sheaves, do not insult her” (Ruth 2:15).

Luke begins the story of the church at this feast: “When the day of Pentecost came, they were all together in one place” (Acts 2:1).

Paul calls the risen Christ “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). Some Christians see a match with the first sheaf lifted up on the day after the Sabbath. The Gospels themselves do not draw that link.
passages.asks: The harvest feast had a law for the poor set in the middle of it. Ask whether your times of celebration and plenty have room in them for people who have little. And ask what ‘first sheaf’ of your income or time you could give before you use the rest.

passages.t: Trumpets, and the Day of Atonement
passages.happening:
“On the first day of the seventh month you are to have a day of rest, a sacred assembly announced by trumpet blasts” (verse 24).

“The tenth day of this seventh month is the Day of Atonement. You shall hold a sacred assembly and humble yourselves” (verse 27). No work at all is to be done, “for it is the Day of Atonement, when atonement is made for you before the LORD your God” (verse 28).

“It will be a Sabbath of complete rest for you, and you shall humble yourselves. From the evening of the ninth day of the month until the following evening you are to keep your Sabbath” (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
The seventh month falls in September or October. It closed the farming year, when grapes, olives and other fruit were gathered in. It held three feasts.

The first is a day of rest announced with trumpets. Leviticus says little more about it. In later Jewish life this day became Rosh Hashanah, the New Year. The text calls it only a day of rest and trumpet blasts.

Ten days later comes the Day of Atonement, the day of chapter 16. That chapter told what the high priest did. This one tells what the people did. They gathered, they did no work at all, and they humbled themselves, which Israel understood as fasting.

The day ran ‘from the evening ... until the following evening’. In Israel a day began at sunset. Jewish communities keep the day in this way still, from one evening to the next. It is Yom Kippur.

The words are strong. Anyone who would not keep the day cut himself off from his people. The whole nation stopped together, to be made clean together.
passages.later:
The yearly day is described in full earlier in this book: “on this day atonement will be made for you to cleanse you, and you will be clean from all your sins before the LORD” (Leviticus 16:30).

The letter to the Hebrews speaks of a rest that still lies ahead: “There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9).

Some Christians link the trumpets of the seventh month with the trumpet the New Testament speaks of at Christ's return. That is a link of theme. The New Testament does not state it.
passages.asks: Once a year a whole people stopped everything to be honest before God about its sins. Ask when you last set aside real time to look at your life before God. And ask what a community, a family or a church, might gain from doing that together.

passages.happening:
“On the fifteenth day of the seventh month the Feast of Tabernacles to the LORD begins, and it continues for seven days” (verse 34). The first day and the eighth are days of rest and assembly (verses 35-36, 39).

“On the first day you are to gather the fruit of majestic trees, the branches of palm trees, and the boughs of leafy trees and of willows of the brook. And you are to rejoice before the LORD your God for seven days” (verse 40).

“You are to dwell in booths for seven days”, the reason being “so that your descendants may know that I made the Israelites dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt” (verses 42-43).
passages.hearers:
Five days after the most solemn day of the year comes the most joyful week. The order matters: first the people are made clean, then they rejoice.

For seven days every family lived in a booth, a rough shelter of branches. The Hebrew word is sukkah, and the feast is called Sukkot. The harvest was in and the barns were full. Just then Israel moved out of its houses and into shelters that could not keep out the wind.

The reason is memory. Their fathers had lived in the wilderness with nothing more lasting than tents, and God had kept them. The booth said: what you have is a gift, and you have lived on less.

And they were told to rejoice. Joy is commanded here. Later Jewish practice took the ‘fruit of majestic trees’ to be the citron, and waved it with branches of palm, myrtle and willow. Jewish families build and eat in such shelters every year to this day.

Should Christians keep these feasts? Christians have answered in different ways. Most churches hold that the feasts, like the sacrifices, belonged to the covenant of Sinai and were fulfilled in Christ, and they leave the keeping of special days to conscience (Romans 14:5-6). Yet the church's own year grew out of this one. Easter is tied to Passover, and Pentecost keeps its name and its place fifty days later. Other Christians, among them many Jewish believers in Jesus, keep the feasts as a way of honoring what Jesus himself kept, though not as a condition of being accepted by God. These notes take no side.
passages.later:
After the exile the returned people kept this feast with great joy: “The whole assembly who had returned from exile made booths and lived in them” (Nehemiah 8:17).

Deuteronomy says who is to share the joy: “you, your sons and daughters, your menservants and maidservants, and the Levite, as well as the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widows among you” (Deuteronomy 16:14).

At this feast Jesus stood up in the temple and called out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink” (John 7:37).

Paul writes to the Colossians about feasts, new moons and Sabbaths: “These are a shadow of the things to come” (Colossians 2:17). As the notes on that letter say, a shadow is real. It shows the shape of something. Paul does not call these days bad.
passages.asks: With the barns full, Israel went and lived in a shelter of branches to remember that everything it had was given. Ask what would remind you of that. And ask whether your faith has room for commanded joy: a time simply to be glad before God for what he has done.
